seoTitle: Bernoulli equation Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Bernoulli equation: work out fluid density from the pressure and the height. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the pressure, the height and the fluid speed and the Bernoulli equation calculator solves for fluid density. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Bernoulli equation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bernoulli equation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fluid density in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the pressure (Position 1 parameters), the height (Position 1 parameters), the fluid speed (Position 1 parameters) and the height (Position 2 parameters).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bernoulli equation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fluid density=2 × (-pressure + pressure) ÷ (2 × gravitational acceleration × height − 2 × gravitational acceleration × height + (fluid speed ^ 2) − (fluid speed ^ 2))
Pressure=pressure + pressure change
Volumetric flow rate=mass flow rate ÷ fluid density
Pipe diameter at position 1=2 × the square root of (volumetric flow rate ÷ fluid speed) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Volumetric flow rate=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × (pipe diameter at position 2 ^ 2) × fluid speed

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Pressure = 10 Pa, Pressure change = 10 Pa and Gravitational acceleration = 9.8067 g. The calculator returns Pressure = 20 Pa.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Pressure = 20 Pa should be roughly the size you expected from Pressure = 10 Pa and Pressure change = 10 Pa.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Pressure, opening in pascals

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bernoulli equation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the pressure, the height and the fluid speed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bernoulli equation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fluid density, derived from the pressure, the height and the fluid speed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bernoulli equation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pressure, the height and the fluid speed, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter fluid density in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Fluid density opens in kilograms per cubic meter and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Pressure = 20 Pa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bernoulli equation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
